content.thinking:
I'm thinking parts without explicit joints should attach to a root joint at the origin, with a dedicated "lidHinge" joint so the chest lid can swing open. Now I'm sketching the overall design direction: exaggerated, dynamic League of Legends-style shapes with bold, saturated color accents.

I'm planning the hoard's contents and layout: a coin mound, open chest overflowing with gold, crown, goblets, gems, urns, necklaces, rings, and a glowing relic orb, sized around 1.8m across with the chest near 0.9m wide, sitting on a dark purple octagonal stone dais with gold rune inlays. I'm settling on a palette of deep purple-navy stone, rich gold, and glowing hextech-cyan gems with magenta, emerald, and ruby accents for strong contrast, then working out the top-down coordinate layout for the base and coin mound geometry.

Thinking through coin texturing for performance...

Better approach: split coins into a flat-colored body part merged separately from textured cap discs placed slightly above, keeping parts simple while varying the face emblem textures across coins.

Now moving to the chest — a large ornate piece at the back-left with a hinged open lid. I'm planning the body as a wood-painted box with gold banding, corner brackets, and a lock plate glowing cyan at the keyhole, while figuring out how to shape the curved lid using a lathe or swept cylinder section.

For the hinge mechanics, I'll build the lid parts in their closed position attached to a hinge joint, then rotate that joint about the back edge by roughly -110° to swing it open, working out the correct sign of rotation so the lid lifts up and back rather than into the box.

Now I'm thinking through the chest's filled interior with a gold coin mound and gems, plus a crimson velvet lining on the underside of the lid. I'm also sketching out the overall proportions—width, depth, body height, and an arched lid—with chunky, flared League-style gold corner accents.

For placement, I'm considering giving the chest a slight yaw rotation for visual liveliness rather than keeping it strictly axis-aligned, which means I'd need a small coordinate helper to transform local chest-frame points into world space for each part.

For the lid joint, I'll figure out rotation around the chest's local axis by computing it from the yaw-rotated frame rather than a fixed world axis. Now I'm planning the dais itself: a dark purple octagonal rock slab with a lathed shape, gold rim trim, rune paint on top, and scattered low-poly rock chunks around the edge plus a floor ring.

For the runes on top, I'm adding a glowing cyan decal as a flat textured ring with hextech circle patterns, positioned so it reads well from above but stays visible outside the coin radius (0.85–1.05) rather than getting buried.

For the coin mound, I'm building it as a lathed hill shape with mottled gold paint, with a main mound and a smaller secondary mound near the chest, then scattering coins across the top using a height function combining several bump contributions.

For the mound surface itself, I'm generating a custom low-poly heightfield mesh (28x28 grid over 2m) with flat shading and gold paint, tilting coin normals based on the surface gradient and tapering the edges smoothly to a circular outline. I'm also considering a separate smaller heightfield slab inside the chest to hold its own pile of coins.

I'm now sketching the height function as a sum of several bumps: a large hill near one side, a secondary hill behind it, a spill shape near the chest's front lip, and another hill further back, all blended with a minimal base value and fading to zero past a 1.05 radius from center.

I also need to handle mesh placement on top of the dais at y=0.1 — since vertices sitting at zero height would coincide exactly with the dais plane and cause z-fighting, I'll either add a tiny offset or skip rendering triangles whose corner heights are all near zero. For the chest itself, I'm positioning it at roughly (-0.3, 0.1, -0.45) with a body height around 0.5 and the lid raised open to about 0.95 total height.

Now I'm designing the crown that sits on the main mound near (0.35, _, 0.25), about 0.3m wide and tilted slightly. It'll have a tapered gold base band with a jewel row, five spiky flame-shaped points extruded around the ring, a crimson velvet inner cap, and a glowing magenta central gem — building each point using tangent and up vectors computed from its angular position on the circle.

I'm setting up a local coordinate frame class with origin, orientation, and point/direction helpers so I can build the crown geometry relative to its own tilted transform rather than world space, plus starting helper functions like a box builder that uses this frame.

Chest lid items get bone: LID, and I'll wrap options with a helper defaulting to bone: ROOT to reduce repetition. Next I'm planning the goblets — 3-4 of them, including a gold goblet standing upright on the dais built as a lathe shape with a gem band.

I'm designing a custom gold paint function that shades based on surface normal, mixing dark and base tones with a smoothstep against the light direction and adding edge highlights, aiming for a hard-edged LoL-style look with painted gradient accents.

I'll go with my own three-tone banded metal paint plus noise streaks instead of a toon kit, since it gives a better hand-painted feel. To keep texture resolution manageable, I'm limiting painted shading to key elements like the gold metal, mound, wood chest, stone dais, and goblets, while coins and small props just use flat colors from a tight 64-color palette, with paint resolution set to 2048 for sharper detail.

Checking the math on texel density confirms 2048 gives plenty of sharpness even across a 15 m² painted area, so I'll settle on that size. For the gems, I'm planning lathe-cut crystal shapes with crown and pavilion facets plus clustered hex-prism crystals, each colored distinctly (ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz, aquamarine) and given a glow effect, with separate materials per gem color.

I'm weighing whether full emissive glow would flatten facet shading and make the gems look less faceted, so maybe only reserve glow for standout pieces like hextech crystal clusters and the crown's centerpiece gem while keeping most other gems non-glowing to preserve detail.

I'm reading "nothing hangs above it" as no detached floating parts below the floor line, so I'll allow a small cluster of floating diamond motes near the crystal since they're loosely part of the model. Setting gem glow strength to 0.55.

For extras, I'm expanding the prop list beyond coins, gems, chest, and crown: a draped pearl necklace, rings, stacked stamped gold ingots, maybe a potion flask, a treasure map scroll, and a tipped-over coin sack for variety and heft.

On part budget, since parts are essentially free below 1000, I don't need to merge everything by colour just to hit a lower count — coins alone could be a few hundred individually, which fits the "prop group" detail target without forced merging.

I'll merge the coin swarm and studs into grouped meshes, but keep gems, goblets, and crown pieces as individual parts, aiming for roughly 400-600 total. For triangle budget, octagonal coin cylinders at ~28 tris each across 450 coins land around 16k, well within the 60k limit, and I'll texture coin faces with an SVG emblem using circular UV mapping.

I'm designing coin face geometry oriented upward and offset slightly above the cylinder, grouping by texture into gold, silver, and copper variants with distinct palette colors, while keeping the cylinder bodies flat-colored.

For standing or leaning coins, I'll add both top and bottom faces, though I'll skip the bottom face unless the tilt angle is large enough to expose it, saving triangle cost. I'm scaling up coin size into a stylized, chunky 8-10cm diameter rather than realistic proportions, fitting a radius around 0.055-0.06 for the hoard dais, with the underlying hill surface painted gold-mottled to match.

For scattering coins across the hill, I'm using rejection sampling with a minimum distance to approximate a poisson distribution, picking random x,z within the dais radius and sampling height from the heightfield, requiring a minimum elevation so most coins land on the mound with a few scattered near the periphery floor. Each coin gets a tilt derived from the surface gradient plus random jitter, random yaw, and is sunk slightly into the surface to avoid floating; I'm relaxing the minimum distance to allow some overlap since random tilts and height jitter prevent z-fighting, aiming for roughly 450 coins across the hills.

I'm extending this to the chest interior, building a separate bumpy heightfield in the chest's local coordinates for coins to scatter onto inside the cavity, writing a generic `scatterCoins(sampler, n, seed)` function that takes any surface sampler returning a point and normal so it works for both the hill and the chest interior.

For the chest lid, I'm considering adding a glowing cyan rune sigil decal on the velvet-and-gold-trimmed underside, deciding on an open angle around 95–100° so the top-down view reveals enough of the interior glow without overcomplicating it with volumetric lighting, and now I'm defining the chest's local dimensions like width and depth.

I'm now building the chest body as a shell made of four wall boxes plus a bottom and an interior fill heightfield, planning to paint wood grain and vertical plank stripes by converting world-space points into the chest's local coordinate frame inside the paint closure so the bands stay aligned despite yaw, while noting that since paint only sets albedo under standard lighting, any shading I bake into the paint function is additive on top of the real lighting rather than a replacement for it.

For the color palette, I'm leaning toward a LoL-flavored scheme: deep indigo-purple wood planks with gold banding and cyan magical accents for an Arcane/Ahri feel, but I want to avoid an all-purple chest-on-purple-dais look, so I'm shifting the dais to a slate teal-blue stone with cyan runes to contrast against the purple-and-gold chest.

Keeping the camera top-down so the chest's silhouette and pile shape stay readable at a glance. For details, I want the body in wood plum with gold corner brackets—extruded L-shapes with rivets—and horizontal gold bands wrapping the box.

Feet are tiny gold ball-and-claw shapes, sphere with cone claws, which feels charmingly ornate for the scale. The front gets a big gold shield-shaped lock plate with a glowing cyan keyhole gem and hasp, and the lid is an arched half-cylinder hinged at the back top edge, sized to span the chest's depth.

Now I'm working through how to build that arched lid as a shell with real thickness—essentially extruding a crescent-shaped profile (outer arc plus an inset inner arc) along the width so it forms a hollow curved band rather than a solid block.

I realize the crescent extrusion only caps the ends with crescent-shaped faces, leaving the semicircular interior open, so I need separate half-disc plates at each end to close it properly. Alternatively, I could simplify by making the lid a solid half-ellipse prism with a flat underside, then just adding a thin crimson plate on that underside to represent the velvet lining.

For the lid itself, I'm shaping it as a half-ellipse prism with semi-axes 0.30 and 0.26, built from a 14-point polygon with a slight bevel, and smooth shading for the curved surface. For the gold bands decorating the arch, I'm placing thin crescent-profile strips at a few x positions, scaling the outer edge slightly larger than the lid surface so the bands sit proud of it while the inner edge matches the lid contour.

Now I'm working through the hinge geometry: the lid's local origin sits at the back hinge point, with z running front-to-back and y running vertically, and the band's slab occupies a narrow x-range that stays hidden inside the lid solid except for the protruding strip. I'm also adding a thin crimson lining plate at the lid's flat underside near the hinge frame, making sure the arch outline coordinates run correctly from z=0 to z=D.

All lid parts are built in the closed pose attached to a LID bone, which needs a joint created at the hinge point so the pose rotation works correctly. For decoration, I'm planning a crimson velvet underside plate with a quilted diamond pattern, gold trim border rods, and a glowing rune sigil centered on it, sized roughly 0.9×0.5 within the lid's 0.6-depth footprint—then moving on to the chest body's front lock plate and side handles.

Now I'm adding side iron rings with brackets and rows of merged gold studs, then working out the coin pile mound filling the chest's interior cavity—a dome rising from the rim height up toward the center, with a spilling bump at the front edge that extends over the lip toward the dais, treated as part of the hidden world heightfield colliding with the chest walls.

I need to cap the spill bump's peak height below the chest wall and keep it near the front, excluding coin scatter points that fall inside the chest or crown footprints. Now I'm laying out the overall world positions — dais center at origin, dais top at y=0.12 as the baseline, and placing the chest at roughly (-0.30, G...).

Continuing the layout, I'm figuring the chest's yaw to angle its front toward the camera, then placing the main coin hill, the leaning crown on top of it, the tall hextech crystal cluster in the back-right, and the goblets resting on the dais near the chest.

Now I'm positioning the remaining vessels — a tipped silver goblet with spilling coins, an upright jeweled chalice on the hill, and a small standing goblet — aiming for a mix of three upright pieces and one tipped over, plus working out where a tipped moneybag sack can sit near the chest's left rear without overlapping the dais edge.

I'm then planning a stacked ingot pyramid for the front-right, and figuring out how to drape a beaded necklace with a pendant gem from the chest lip down onto the hill, deciding it's simpler to lay it as a curved loop resting on the mound surface rather than hanging in space.

I'm adding small torus rings with gems on coins, scattering around forty loose gems across the hoard, surrounding the dais with a ring of faceted boulders and glowing crystals, and sprinkling floating motes. Checking scale, the dais is about 1.25m radius with the hoard spanning roughly 2.4m, which fits a reasonable diorama size.

Now I'm setting up the code imports and helper utilities for building the scene, pulling in math, path, and shading helpers.

I'm defining a metal shading function that uses a light direction vector and noise-based banding to create a cel-shaded look with distinct dark, mid, and light bands based on surface normal dot products.

I'm also adding a subtle teal bounce-light tint for undersides facing downward, simulating ambient reflection from the glow source, and planning a cracked-stone texture using cellular noise for the dais material.

For wood, I'm indexing planks along the local X axis with hashed color variation per plank, then faking anisotropic grain by stretching the noise sampling along the plank direction.

For wall orientation I'm choosing between the lx and lz coordinate based on which world axis the normal most aligns with, so planks run the right direction on each face.

For the velvet lining I'm mapping local lid coordinates to lid-local u,v since the paint gets baked in the closed pose before any later rotation.

I'm plotting the tufted-diamond pattern using modular distance checks on lx+lz to place quilt lines, then adding tiny golden dots at the diamond intersections for buttons, checking that the texel resolution is fine enough to resolve them. Now I'm sketching out the coin face textures — distinguishing gold, silver, and copper variants by rim, field, and emblem colors, and writing an SVG generator function...

Writing SVG code...

For the gem geometry, I'm working out how to build cut-gem shapes using lathe geometry for brilliant cuts, scaled octahedrons, chamfered boxes for emerald cuts, and hex prisms with pointed caps for crystal shards, all with flat shading and randomized orientation.

Now I'm adding a gem placement helper that creates each gem as its own glowing part attached to the root bone, plus small sparkle quad cards facing the camera to add highlight accents on the gems.

Writing heightfield bump function...

Still placing bumps...

Now I'm setting up the heightfield mesh grid at roughly 31×31 resolution, then adding small hash-based jitter to vertex heights for a lumpy, faceted surface look rather than a perfectly smooth analytic shape.

For coin placement, I'm computing each coin's resting height from the mesh surface including jitter, using smooth noise sampling so coins sit naturally into dips and bumps rather than floating or sinking unrealistically, accounting for the roughly 1.2cm coin thickness against the small jitter amplitude.

Actually, a cleaner approach: using the surface ray-casting API to shoot rays downward at each scatter position and get exact hit points plus normals directly from the hill mesh, which is far more accurate than approximating via bilinear interpolation and still cheap at roughly 450 rays.

For orientation, I'll align each coin's local Y-axis to the surface normal using an `aim` helper, then multiply in a random spin rotation about that same local Y for yaw variation, avoiding the discouraged direct quaternion setup. Coin geometry gets placed by cloning and transforming the base geometry into position before merging everything into one mesh.

I'm grouping parts by color so I can merge coin bodies (faceted octagonal cylinders) and face/edge details (slightly smaller circles offset above the top face) separately, matching index structures so the merges stay valid, and flattening normals where a low-poly faceted look is wanted.

For standing coins, I'll give about 15% of them a steep edge-on tilt (75-85°) so they look like they're leaning against piles, and add bottom faces only for those steep ones to avoid wasted geometry. I'm setting the total coin count to around 500 based on the hill's surface area, and now I'm starting the goblet builder function.

I'm sketching the goblet's lathe profile as a series of (radius, height) points moving from the foot up through the stem, knop, and into the bowl, then defining the interior wall points so the bowl reads as hollow rather than solid.

I want to add filled contents inside the cup -- either a dome of coins/gems or a glowing liquid disc -- so one goblet could hold a magenta elixir and another an overflowing mound of treasure, and I'm bumping the overall scale up for a chunkier, more stylized look.

Now I'm thinking through surface ornamentation: a ring of gems around the bowl, engraved rim lines made from thin swept torus shapes, ridge detailing baked into the lathe profile, and vertical flutes painted using the angular parameter so the metal paint function can optionally render fluting every 30 degrees. I'll default the lathe to 12 segments for smoothness, with 8 as a chunkier alternative.

I'm settling on 10 lathe segments for a lightly faceted goblet look, then moving to a tipped variant tilted 80° around Z with a few coins scattered near the mouth along an arc. For the crown, I'm designing a chunky base band around 13cm radius with a moulded lathe profile -- defining the outer and inner ring points that create the stepped, grooved shape of the band before adding the spires on top.

Since the band's interior would otherwise look hollow when tilted, I'm adding a crimson velvet dome liner that bulges up between the crown's points, with a lathe profile curving from the rim up to a rounded peak -- plus gold arch bands sweeping over the dome from front to back to complete the royal look.

Now I'm designing seven alternating tall and short spires (flame/trefoil shaped, gold-beveled, each set with a gem and topped by a small orb), leaning slightly outward for drama, along with arches meeting at a glowing cyan centerpiece gem.

Defining spire geometry...

Placing alternating gems between spires on the band, pearl spheres on short spire tips and ruby on others, then sketching two catmull-smoothed arches sweeping from opposite band points over the dome to a top orb apex.

Instead of a cross, I'll top it with a glowing cyan hextech-style octahedron crystal for a League of Legends feel. I'm tilting the crown by rotating it slightly off-axis and resting it on the hill so its base sinks into the coin pile, with nearby coins overlapping the rim for realism, and sizing it a bit chunkier relative to the spires. For the chest, I'm adding a glowing hexagonal gem with a keyhole lock plate extruded in gold on the front face.

Writing lock and hinge geometry...

Now I'm designing a hextech crystal cluster — five hexagonal-prism crystals of varying sizes tilted outward, translucent and glowing cyan, each seated on a stone base with a gold collar, with inner core lines added for a faceted lit effect.

I'm adding two-tone glow to each crystal (cyan body, lighter glowing tip), plus six small floating octahedra shards around the cluster at varying heights and a thin gold-and-cyan rune ring tilted and orbiting the crystals, topped off with an octagonal lathe-profile dais base.

Working out the dais geometry now — defining the stepped octagon outline for the lathe profile and matching a trim ring to its vertex angles, then switching to a smoother 16-segment lathe to avoid alignment mismatches.

The ring texture should have concentric cyan lines with rune glyph ticks and gear-teeth accents, glowing at strength 1 so only the uncovered edges peek through around the hoard — good for a top-down read. I'll render it as a 512px SVG with viewBox 200, giving roughly 2.56px per unit so a 1.5 stroke width comes out around 3.8px, nice and crisp. For the dais periphery I'm planning low flat-shaded icosahedron rocks at detail 0.

I want to add gold corner studs with small cyan gems at each of the octagon's 8 vertices for the dais, plus scatter around 46 gems of varying sizes across the hill using ray-based positions. Now I'm defining a gem geometry function that builds a lathe-based brilliant-cut gem shape with a pointed pavilion tip.

Writing gem geometry variants...

I'll limit the gem types to brilliant, octa, emerald, and shard, and now I'm working out placement logic: positioning each gem slightly sunk into the surface along the normal, orienting it to aim along that normal with some spin, and adding a random tilt for natural variation.

I'm picking a seven-color flat palette for gem types—ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz, aqua, and diamond—while keeping an eye on the overall color budget alongside the gold, silver, wood, and ink tones already in use. Now I'm designing the moneybag as a lathe-profile shape: wide at the bottom, narrowing at the neck, flaring at the top, in a burlap tan tone.

I'm settling on a teal sack contrasted with a gold drawstring tie and coin emblem patch, tilted on its side with the mouth spilling coins forward. Writing lathe profile coordinates...

For the ingots, I'm building trapezoid prisms sized small, tapered narrower at top, painted bright gold with a darker stamped emblem plate inset on top, arranging eight as a 3-2-1 pyramid plus a couple toppled over for variety. Now moving on to the necklace, threading pearls along a closed catmull-rom path.

For the pearls, I'm sampling the hill-surface path at thirty points, placing small white-lavender spheres along it, adding a thin gold thread and a pendant with a big aqua teardrop gem in a gold setting, with the loop positioned using ray-cast points around the hill. Then for rings, I'm placing three gold torus shapes with gems on top of the pile, positioned via surface raycasts.

Now I'm adding gold ring handles on the chest's end faces plus sparkling star accents, and designing the chest lid with a gem-studded band along the front center and a large magenta cabochon, along with gold scroll filigree rendered as an SVG decal texture on the front panel.

Writing SVG scroll decal...

I'm also planning gold ball feet at the four corners, a gold plinth trim around the base wider than the walls, and setting the chest's local dimensions to roughly 1.0 wide, 0.6 deep, and 0.46 tall.

Now I'm working out the gold banding placement -- vertical straps on the front and sides, a horizontal rim band near the top, and a matching bottom trim, each protruding slightly from the wood surface. I'm also setting up the lid's dome geometry as a semi-ellipse arching above the body, and figuring out the hinge joint coordinates where the lid attaches at the back of the chest.

I'm now checking the rotation math for the lid swinging open about the hinge axis, verifying the sign of the angle by tracing where the lid's top apex point ends up after rotating roughly -105 degrees, confirming it swings backward correctly rather than into the chest body.

At 105° the lid's back edge clears the chest's rear wall with no collision, so maybe dialing back to 100° is safer. Checking ground contact, the dais bottom sits at y=0 and its top at y=0.12, so everything stays above ground properly. Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy with the root and lid joints and their positions.

Confirming just two joints are needed—root and lid hinge—with the lid role tagged as "hinge" and root type properly bound to the full mesh. Writing a helper transform class to convert local box coordinates into world-space points and directions using position, rotation, and quaternion math...

Adding box-building helpers...

Still defining the bevel helper...

Now I'm sketching a tube/sweep helper for thin rounded strokes along a path, and considering a bucket-based merge strategy to batch coin geometries by material key before flushing them into combined parts.

I'm working out the gold paint palette with distinct dark, mid, and light tones for shading, plus flatter accent colors for individual coins, then thinking through how shared metal paints affect atlas texel density across all the painted surfaces like the hill and dais.

For the hill's coin pile surface, I'm using a cell-based noise pattern that toggles between mid and dark gold tones with darkened edges, so it reads visually like a mass of coins rather than a smooth surface. Now I'm ready to write out all the final code carefully, including a typed tuple for 3D vectors.

Setting up imports and palette constants...

Still defining color bands...

Writing wood grain function...

Now I'm setting up a heightfield with randomized bumps across a grid, defining the sampling resolution and spacing for the terrain-like surface.

Skipped triangles mean zero height there, which is fine since nothing's drawn. For scattering coins on the hill, I'm casting rays downward from above the hill surface to find landing points, while excluding footprints around the chest and other objects (crown, goblets, sack, ingots, crystal base) using local coordinate bounds and keep-out radii.

I'm reconsidering how strict those exclusions need to be — slight overlaps near goblet feet or crown rims are probably fine since those pieces naturally sink into the coin pile, so only the ingots and goblet bases really need clearance to avoid looking wrong.

Now I'm working out item placement using the hill's surface raycast to find each object's resting height and orientation — crown position blends the world up-axis with the surface normal for a natural lean, and then I need to figure out how coins placed inside the chest interior should be sampled in the chest's local coordinate space so they sit correctly relative to its rotated footprint.

For the chest interior, I'm building a small heightfield grid in local coordinates that domes up toward the center and dips near the rim, staying just low enough that the chest walls hide the edges, while the front lip needs to blend into the spill pile outside so the transition reads as one continuous mound.

Still working out the dome and cascade height formulas...

This is getting too fiddly mathematically, so I think I'll simplify by letting the chest-spill bump and interior dome handle most of it, then add a separate small wedge-shaped mesh for the coins spilling over the lip, shaping its cross-section profile from inside the chest down to the outer slope.

Checking the chest walls aren't part of the surface set, so rays over wall footprint hit the hidden hill underneath instead, and since the hill's spill bump stays below wall height, those coins end up hidden anyway—so I should just filter out coin placements that fall within the wall footprint ring to avoid wasted samples.

I'm separating the coin sampling into three distinct domains: hill coins (excluding the chest footprint box and a tongue-adjacent strip), interior coins scattered within the interior region, and tongue coins placed along the tongue domain, each sampled against their own surface. The camera's default three-quarter angle should show the chest front fine since it faces roughly +Z.

For quantities I'm settling on 420 hill coins, 90 interior, 40 tongue, plus 40 hill gems and 8 interior gems. Coins get weighted random colours (gold A 45%, gold B 30%, copper-gold 15%, silver 10%), each paired with its own small face texture carrying a distinct emblem, while the coin bodies stay flat-colored and rely on lighting plus the face textures for visual variety, all seeded with a fixed rng.

For sparkles I'm designing small glowing star-shaped planes oriented toward the camera using a fixed direction vector, placed with consistent aim-axis orientation, and planning a handful of floating diamond particles near the crystal cluster later. Now I'm working out the hextech crystal cluster itself — positioning a main crystal and several smaller companions around it with varying radius, height, tilt, and azimuth, building each as a hex prism with a tapered tip, considering a lathe-based profile for the shape.

I'm adding gold claw-like prongs gripping the crystal base along with a chunky navy rock piece, and checking that the cyan glow strength keeps the crystals' faceted shading readable rather than flattening them into silhouettes. Next I'm placing a hextech sigil design on the underside of the lid, positioning a glowing plane just beneath the lid's flat bottom surface.

Working out the lining plate dimensions and position, since it needs to sit flush within the lid without colliding with the interior pile once I account for the open-pose geometry (closed-lid collisions don't matter since only the open pose renders). Positioning the sigil plane just below the lining's outer face, facing downward.

I'm sketching a helper function for generating gem geometries by kind, starting with the "cut" type using a lathe profile...

Scaling the octahedron non-uniformly, then sketching an emerald-cut shape with a stacked crown and pavilion using cylinders and a cone merged together.

I'll use LatheGeometry for all the cut/step/shard shapes rather than merging cylinders. Then I'm writing a helper function to create gem parts with a bone transform and optional glow effect, plus a `layGem` helper to position gems directly onto a surface hit point.

Writing crown spire geometry...

Adjusting spire orientation...

For the crown dome, I'm choosing a flat velvet-like color instead of trying to fake quilting texture. I'm sketching the two decorative arches as curved sweeps using a few control points that follow the dome's profile, making sure the apex height and dome height line up so there's no visible gap.

Writing sweep geometry...

Adding the glowing disc and coin mound details, plus gems on top, and figuring out how to tilt a goblet so it lies on the hill with coins spilling out of its mouth along the horizontal axis.

Now setting origin at the goblet midpoint raised slightly, then moving on to the sack, ingots, necklace, rings, rocks, and dais gems. I'm planning to write the full file incrementally and verify with typecheck and preview as I go, starting with SVG texture generation for coin faces using layered circles for rim, groove, and field colors.

Designing emblem shapes per coin type — a star for gold, crescent for silver, shield for copper — along with a helper function to compute star polygon points, plus a sparkle texture using a four-point star path and glow, and starting on the dais ring texture.

I'm positioning the circle plane on the dais octagon so it inscribes properly above the top surface, then sketching gold filigree scroll paths for the chest decoration, sizing strokes to render cleanly at the target resolution.

Skipping the rune letters idea. I'm scattering 14 small coins on the dais floor, avoiding the raised hill areas, and placing a ring of low rocks just beyond the dais edge to extend the scene naturally while keeping the overall footprint within a reasonable scale.

I'm setting up helper functions for extruded plates and beveled boxes, along with rotation utilities and paint color typing, to build out the geometry pieces efficiently.

Now I'm drafting the full build script, starting with creating the treasureHoard builder and defining root and lid joints with their positions, directions, and hinge roles.

input.command: cd ~/tmp-archive/sonnet-100/treasureHoardSonnet/ && sed -n 1,80p kits/glow.ts; sed -n 120,215p src/builder.ts; grep -n "mergeGeometries" -r src | head -3; ls node_modules/three/examples/jsm/utils | head -3
